# One more characterization  {#secquantiles background-color="#1c191c"}

## 

So far we have seen several characterizations of probability distributions:

- Cumulative distribution functions

- Probability generating functions

- Characteristic functions

. . .

<!-- The last characterization is praised for its behaviour with respect to sums of independent random variables. -->

For _univariate distributions_, a companion to the cumulative distribution function is the _quantile function_.

::: {.notes}
The quantile function plays a significant role in simulations, statistics and risk theory.
:::

# Quantile functions of discrete distributions  {#seqquantdiscrete background-color="#1c191c"}


## 

The quantile transformation has many applications. It can be used to show stochastic domination properties.

::: {#exm-quantile-discrete}

### Discrete and mixed distributions

The quantile function of a discrete distribution is a step function that jumps at the cumulative probability of every possible outcome.

If a probability distribution is a mixture of a discrete distribution and a continuous distribution, the quantile function jumps at the cumulative probability of every possible outcome of the discrete component.

:::

::: {.notes}
@fig-quantiles, @fig-quantiles2, @fig-quantiles3 and @fig-quantiles4 illustrate quantile functions for discrete (binomial) distributions and for distributions that are neither discrete nor continuous.
:::

## Quantile functions of clipped Gaussians

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Quantile functions of clipped Gaussians](cm-14-quantile-functions_files/figure-revealjs/fig-quantiles2-1.png){#fig-quantiles2 width=576}
:::
:::


Quantile functions of

$$\max(X, \tau) \text{ where } X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$$

for $\tau \in \{0, -1\}$.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

The quantile function of $\max(X,\tau)$ is

$$\mathbb{I}_{(0,\Phi(\tau))}(p) \times \tau + \Phi^{\leftarrow}(p) \times \mathbb{I}_{(\Phi(\tau), 1)}(p)$$

or

$$\Phi^{\leftarrow}(p \vee \Phi(\tau))$$

The two distributions are neither absolutely continuous nor discrete.

:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Let $\Phi^\leftarrow$ denote the quantile function of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.
:::

## Cumulative distribution functions

::: {#def-cdf}

### Cumulative distribution function

A cumulative distribution function $F$ is

- non-negative

- $[0,1]$-valued

- non-decreasing

- right-continuous, with a left limit at any point.

:::

::: {.callout-tip}
The cumulative distribution function of a diffuse probability measure is continuous at any point.
:::

## Quantile function

The quantile function $F^{\leftarrow}$ is defined as an _extended inverse_ of the cumulative distribution function $F$.

::: {#def-quantile}

### Quantile function

The quantile function $F^{\leftarrow}$ of a random variable $X$ distributed according to $P$ (with cumulative distribution function $F$) is defined as

$$\begin{array}{rl}
F^{\leftarrow} (p)
   & = \inf \Big\{ x : P\{X \leq x\} \geq p \Big\} \\
   & = \inf \Big\{ x : F (x) \geq p \Big\} \qquad \text{for } p \in (0,1).
\end{array}$$

:::

## Elementary properties

::: {.callout-warning}
The quantile function is non-decreasing and left-continuous.
:::

## Interplay between $F$ and $F^{\leftarrow}$

The interplay between the quantile and cumulative distribution functions is summarized in the next proposition.

::: {#prp-quantile-cdf}

### Quantile function and CDF

If $F$ and $F^\leftarrow$ are the CDF and the quantile function of (the distribution of) $X$, the following statements hold for $p \in\, ]0, 1[$:

1. $p \leq F(x)$ iff $F^\leftarrow(p) \leq x$

2. $F \circ F^\leftarrow(p) \geq p$

3. $F^\leftarrow \circ F(x) \leq x$

4. If $F ⊴ \text{Lebesgue}$, then $F \circ F^\leftarrow(p) = p$

:::

## Proof of the interplay

::: {.proof}

According to the definition of $F^\leftarrow$, if $F(x) \geq p$ then $F^\leftarrow(p) \leq x$.

. . .

To prove the converse, it suffices to check that $F \circ F^\leftarrow(p) \geq p$.

. . .

Indeed, if $x \geq F^\leftarrow(p)$, as $F$ is non-decreasing, $F(x) \geq F \circ F^\leftarrow(p)$.

If $y = F^\leftarrow(p)$, by definition of $y = F^\leftarrow(p)$

$\exists (z_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $z_n \searrow y$ such that $F(z_n) \geq p$.

But as $F$ is right-continuous, $\lim_n F(z_n) = F(\lim_n z_n) = F(y)$.

Hence $F(y) \geq p$.

We just proved 1. and 2.

:::

## Proof of the interplay, continued {.smaller}

::: {.proof name="continued"}

3. is an immediate consequence of 1.

Let $p = F(x)$. Hence $p \leq F(x)$, according to 1.

This is equivalent to $F^\leftarrow(p) \leq x$, that is $F^\leftarrow \circ F(x) \leq x$.

4. For every $p$ in $]0, 1[$, $\{ x : p = F(x)\}$ is non-empty (Mean value Theorem).

Let $y = \inf \{ x : p = F(x)\} = F^\leftarrow(p)$.

According to 1., $F(y) \geq p$.

Now, if $(z_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \nearrow y$,

for every $n$, $F(z_n) < p$.

By left-continuity, $F(y) = F(\lim_n \uparrow z_n) = \lim_n F(z_n) \leq p$.

Hence $F(y) = p$, that is $F \circ F^\leftarrow(p) = p$.

:::

# Quantile transformation

## 

::: {#prp-quantile-transform}

### Quantile transformation

If $U$ is uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$, and $F$ is a cumulative distribution function over $\mathbb{R}$, $F^{\leftarrow}(U)$ has cumulative distribution function $F$.

The quantile transformation works whatever the continuity properties of $F$.

:::

## Proof of the quantile transformation

::: {.proof}

$$\begin{array}{rl}
  P\Big\{ F^\leftarrow(U) \leq x \Big\}
  & = P\Big\{ U \leq F(x) \Big\} \\
  & = F(x) \, .
\end{array}$$

:::

## QQ-plots

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Normal QQ-plot of a standard Gaussian sample](cm-14-quantile-functions_files/figure-revealjs/fig-qqplot-1.png){#fig-qqplot width=576}
:::
:::


A popular device for comparing two probability distributions on the real line defined by their cumulative distribution functions $F$ and $G$.

The QQ-plot consists in plotting the function $G^{\leftarrow} \circ F$.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

If the two distributions are the same, the line

$$y = G^{\leftarrow} \circ F(x)$$

should lie below $y=x$, according to @prp-quantile-cdf.

The two lines should coincide if $F=G$ is continuous and increasing.

Here:

- $F = \Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

- $G$ is the empirical distribution of a sample of size $500$ from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

:::

::::

## Probability integral transform

Let us conclude this section with an important observation concerning the behaviour of $F(X)$ when $X \sim P$ with cumulative distribution function $F$.

::: {#cor-pit}

### Probability integral transform

If $X \sim P$ with continuous cumulative distribution function $F$,

then

$F(X)$ and $1 - F(X)$ are uniformly distributed on $[0, 1]$.

:::

::: {#exr-pit}

### Prove the corollary

Prove @cor-pit.

:::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
